q: Does the ACA-DC 2 lactose/galactose (lac/gal) operon architecture and gene content differ from the LMD-9 / CNRZ1066 / LMG18311 reference set in ways that predict industrial acidification-rate biomarkers for dairy starter selection?
basis: REPORT.md establishes ACA-DC 2 as a yogurt starter isolate with a complete circular chromosome (1,731,838 bp, 39.21% GC) and 1,556 curated CDS on par with published S. thermophilus starters. Alexandraki et al. (2017) emphasize its industrial-relevance framing but did not perform a comparative acidification-genotype-to-phenotype mapping across strains. The replication pipeline (NCBI Datasets + PGAP + Prokka) confirmed structural equivalence but did not compare lac/gal operon variants across the S. thermophilus pan-genome, and no fermentation phenotype data were tested.
next_steps: Retrieve the ACA-DC 2 GCA_900094135.1 CDS set + LMD-9/CNRZ1066/LMG18311/ND03 reference genomes from NCBI Datasets (free) and extract the lacS/lacZ, galK/galT/galE/galM, lacR loci by orthology (OrthoFinder or Roary --core).
Align promoter, coding, and intergenic regions across the panel to catalog SNPs, indels, and IS-element insertions in lac/gal.

Cross-reference with published S. thermophilus acidification-rate datasets (e.g. Vaughan et al., Delorme et al., Hols et al. reviews) to test whether the ACA-DC 2 lac/gal haplotype clusters with fast- or slow-acidifying industrial strains.
If a signal exists, propose the specific SNP/indel set as a candidate PCR-typing biomarker for starter QC (design primers, estimate cost per assay).

q: Is the two-array, single-spacer CRISPR-Cas configuration observed in ACA-DC 2 a strain-idiosyncratic hallmark, or does it represent a broader phage-defense-barrier bottleneck for industrial S. thermophilus starter longevity in yogurt/mozzarella plants?
basis: REPORT.md confirms via minced (minNR=2) that ACA-DC 2 carries short single-spacer CRISPR arrays at ~849,603-849,704 bp coinciding with the paper's cas-flanked STACADC2_0849 array, and the default minNR=3 finding zero arrays is itself positive evidence for the single-spacer claim. However, the exact count (paper: 2 curated; minced-nr2: 6 candidates) is tool-parameter-sensitive, and the paper did not test how spacer scarcity translates to phage-resistance breadth in dairy-plant conditions where 936/c2/P335-family phages dominate.
next_steps: Rerun the ACA-DC 2 genome through CRISPRCasFinder and CRT in addition to minced, cross-validate array count, and record spacer sequences.
Aggregate CRISPR array count + spacer count from all publicly available S. thermophilus complete genomes (NCBI Datasets 'complete' filter) as a pan-species denominator.
BLAST ACA-DC 2 spacers against public S. thermophilus phage genomes (e.g. NCBI viral genomes; Millard lab phage database) to quantify defended-vs-undefended phage fraction.

Compare with reported industrial phage-outbreak frequency to test the 'sparse CRISPR = shorter production life' hypothesis; propose spacer-augmentation via natural adaptation experiments if warranted.

q: How does the ACA-DC 2 exopolysaccharide (eps) cluster (structure, glycosyltransferase repertoire, priming glycosyltransferase specificity) map onto yogurt-viscosity and mozzarella-melt/stretch texture phenotypes across industrial S. thermophilus starters?
basis: REPORT.md validates the ACA-DC 2 gene inventory (1,556 CDS, 1,850 total genes) to the digit, and Prokka de-novo re-annotation covered structural gene classes, but functional cluster-level analysis of the eps region was not performed in the replication (the 63.89% function-assignment figure from the paper was not reproduced; Prokka default reached 35.9%). Alexandraki et al. describe eps cluster presence qualitatively but do not quantitatively link its architecture to product-texture outcomes.
next_steps: Locate the eps cluster in GCA_900094135.1 by anchoring on epsA/epsB/epsC/epsD conserved genes and defining cluster boundaries by antiSMASH or manual synteny inspection.
Extract the priming glycosyltransferase and downstream GT genes; classify by CAZy family (dbCAN or CAZy web BLAST, both free).
Assemble a small panel of published S. thermophilus eps clusters with linked yogurt-viscosity / mozzarella-stretch measurements from literature (e.g. Broadbent et al., Petersen et al., Zisu & Shah).

Test whether GT-family repertoire or priming-GT identity predicts a texture class (ropy vs non-ropy, high-stretch vs low-stretch); if so, propose a rapid genotype-based texture screen for new isolates.

q: What is the bacteriocin-encoding gene repertoire of ACA-DC 2, and does it predict co-culture compatibility (or antagonism) with the standard yogurt/cheese co-cultures L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and L. helveticus?
basis: REPORT.md notes that BAGEL3 bacteriocin analysis and other qualitative claims (RM systems, stress genes, bacteriocins, whole-genome phylogeny) were 'not independently reproduced this pass' and are explicitly flagged as out of scope. The paper reports bacteriocin features but does not test cross-species inhibition in defined co-culture. This gap is scientifically live because yogurt manufacturing depends on the S. thermophilus + L. bulgaricus proto-cooperation, and a bacteriocin-active starter can silently underperform.
next_steps: Run BAGEL4 (free, current version) and antiSMASH bacteriocin module on GCA_900094135.1 protein set; catalog class I (lantibiotic) and class II bacteriocin candidates with signal peptide and immunity gene predictions.
BLAST candidates against curated bacteriocin databases (BACTIBASE, BAGEL curated set) to assign putative activity spectra.

For each candidate with a predicted Gram-positive spectrum, cross-check against L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus ATCC 11842 and L. helveticus DPC 4571 reference proteomes for known immunity-gene orthologs.
If antagonism is predicted, propose a targeted co-culture growth-curve assay (S. thermophilus + partner) in reconstituted skim milk to test in vitro.

q: Does the pattern of 224 pseudogenes in ACA-DC 2 (functional class distribution, insertion-sequence proximity, orthologous status vs S. salivarius / S. vestibularis) reveal an active genome-reduction trajectory driven by ecological adaptation to the dairy niche?
basis: REPORT.md verifies the 224-pseudogene count exactly (matched by both the deposit-parse and PGAP within variance at 226), a distinctive feature of ACA-DC 2 relative to its congeners. However, functional class analysis of the pseudogenes was not performed in the replication (Prokka function-assignment reached only 35.9%, well below the paper's 63.89%). The paper describes pseudogenes but does not analyze them as a signature of ongoing reductive evolution toward the dairy-milk niche, a well-established pattern in dairy LAB (cf. Douillard et al. on L. helveticus; Bolotin et al. on S. thermophilus vs. S. salivarius).
next_steps: Extract pseudogene coordinates + adjacent regions from the GCF_900094135.1 PGAP GFF (already downloaded per REPORT.md).
Identify orthologs of each pseudogene in S. salivarius CCHSS3 and S. vestibularis F0396 by best-reciprocal BLAST to test whether they were intact in the common ancestor.

Classify functional categories by COG / KEGG / GO enrichment (WebMGA free; eggNOG-mapper free) and test for over-representation of carbohydrate metabolism, transport, or stress-response categories consistent with dairy-niche relaxation of selection.

Map pseudogene-associated IS elements (ISfinder, free) to test whether insertion-sequence expansion is driving the reduction; compare pseudogene density to reported values in other yogurt / cheese starters.
